metadata.title: Time Zones, 24-Hour Time, and Duration
metadata.vcaa_description: Solve problems involving duration, using 12-hour and 24-hour time across multiple time zones
metadata.target_mastery: Convert fluently between 12-hour (am/pm) and 24-hour time, calculate elapsed duration within a day and across midnight, convert times across Australian standard and daylight saving time zones (AWST, ACST, AEST, ACDT, AEDT), and solve international travel duration problems using UTC offsets.
prerequisites: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds ($1\text{ hour} = 60\text{ minutes}$)
Adding and subtracting directed numbers and fractions of an hour

key_vocabulary.definition: A four-digit time notation (`HHMM` or `HH:MM`) running from `0000` (midnight) to `2359` ($11\text{:59 pm}$), eliminating the need for am and pm labels.
The primary global time standard (formerly Greenwich Mean Time, GMT) from which all world time zones are measured as positive (ahead/east) or negative (behind/west) offsets.

Australia has three main standard time zones: Australian Western Standard Time (AWST, $\text{UTC}+8$), Australian Central Standard Time (ACST, $\text{UTC}+9.5$), and Australian Eastern Standard Time (AEST, $\text{UTC}+10$).

Between the first Sunday in October and the first Sunday in April, clocks in SA create ACDT ($\text{UTC}+10.5$) and clocks in VIC, NSW, TAS, and ACT move $1\text{ hour}$ forward to AEDT ($\text{UTC}+11$), while WA, QLD, and NT stay on standard time.

theory.title: Converting Between 12-Hour and 24-Hour Time
theory.explanation: In 12-hour time, the day is split into two $12$-hour periods: **am** (*ante meridiem*, before noon) and **pm** (*post meridiem*, after noon). In 24-hour time, hours are numbered continuously from $00$ to $23$. For morning times from $1\text{:00 am}$ to $11\text{:59 am}$, write a leading zero (`0100` to `1159`). For afternoon/evening times from $1\text{:00 pm}$ to $11\text{:59 pm}$, add $12$ to the hours (`1300` to `2359`). Special cases: $12\text{:00 am}$ (midnight) is `0000` and $12\text{:00 pm}$ (noon) is `1200`.
theory.callout_title: Watch Out for the 12s: Midnight vs Noon
theory.callout_rule: $12\text{:30 am}$ is $30$ minutes after midnight, so it is `0030` (NOT `1230`). $12\text{:30 pm}$ is $30$ minutes after noon, so it stays `1230` (do NOT add $12$ to $12\text{ pm}$).

theory.title: Calculating Elapsed Duration and Crossing Midnight
theory.explanation: Because time uses base $60$ ($1\text{ hour} = 60\text{ minutes}$), never subtract times as ordinary base-$10$ decimals! The safest strategy to find the duration between a start time and an end time is **bridging (chunking) to the next whole hour**, then counting whole hours, or borrowing $1\text{ hour} = 60\text{ minutes}$ when subtracting in 24-hour time. When an event crosses midnight (`24:00` / `00:00`), find the time from start to midnight first, then add the time after midnight.
theory.callout_rule: When subtracting `16:20 - 13:45`, rewrite `16:20` as $15\text{ hours } 80\text{ minutes}$ ($60 + 20 = 80$), then subtract: $(15 - 13)\text{ h } (80 - 45)\text{ min} = 2\text{ h } 35\text{ min}$.

theory.title: Australian Time Zones: Standard Time and Daylight Saving Time
theory.explanation: During winter (Standard Time), Australia uses three zones: **AWST** (WA, $\text{UTC}+8$), **ACST** (SA and NT, $\text{UTC}+9.5$, which is $1.5\text{ h}$ ahead of WA and $0.5\text{ h}$ behind the east), and **AEST** (QLD, NSW, VIC, TAS, ACT, $\text{UTC}+10$, which is $2\text{ h}$ ahead of WA). During summer (Daylight Saving), VIC, NSW, TAS, and ACT advance to **AEDT** ($\text{UTC}+11$) and SA advances to **ACDT** ($\text{UTC}+10.5$), while WA ($\text{UTC}+8$), NT ($\text{UTC}+9.5$), and QLD ($\text{UTC}+10$) do not change their clocks.
theory.callout_title: East is Ahead (+), West is Behind (-)
theory.callout_rule: Moving east towards a larger UTC offset means local clock time is later (add the offset difference); moving west towards a smaller UTC offset means local clock time is earlier (subtract the offset difference).

theory.title: International Flights and Multi-Zone Travel Problems
theory.explanation: To solve flight arrival or duration problems across different time zones, always convert the departure and arrival times into the **same time zone** (either the departure city's local time, the arrival city's local time, or UTC) before adding or subtracting flight duration.
theory.callout_title: Convert to One Common Time Zone First
theory.callout_rule: Never subtract local departure time from local arrival time directly! Convert the departure time into the destination's time zone first, and then add or subtract the flight time.

worked_examples.title: Converting 12-Hour and 24-Hour Times and Finding Duration Across Midnight
worked_examples.problem: An overnight V/Line coach departs Southern Cross Station in Melbourne at $9\text{:45 pm}$ on Friday and arrives in Mildura at $4\text{:20 am}$ on Saturday. (a) Write both the departure and arrival times in 24-hour time. (b) Calculate the total duration of the journey in hours and minutes.

steps.thinking: For $9\text{:45 pm}$, add $12$ to the hours ($9 + 12 = 21$) to get `2145` (or `21:45`). For $4\text{:20 am}$, include a leading zero to get `0420` (or `04:20`).
Bridge across midnight (`24:00`): find the duration from $9\text{:45 pm}$ to midnight, then add the duration from midnight to $4\text{:20 am}$.
steps.working:
$$9\text{:45 pm to } 10\text{:00 pm} = 15\text{ min}; \quad 10\text{:00 pm to midnight} = 2\text{ h} \implies 2\text{ h } 15\text{ min before midnight}$$
$$\text{Total duration} = 2\text{ h } 15\text{ min} + 4\text{ h } 20\text{ min} = 6\text{ hours } 35\text{ minutes}$$

now_you_try.problem: A baker starts her shift at $11\text{:35 pm}$ (`2335`) and finishes at $6\text{:15 am}$ (`0615`) the next morning. How long is her shift in hours and minutes?
now_you_try.hint: Find the time from $11\text{:35 pm}$ to midnight ($25\text{ minutes}$) and add $6\text{ hours } 15\text{ minutes}$.
now_you_try.working_summary: Before midnight: $25\text{ min}$. After midnight: $6\text{ h } 15\text{ min}$. Total $= 6\text{ h } 40\text{ min}$.

worked_examples.title: Converting Times Across Australian Standard and Daylight Saving Zones
worked_examples.problem: An AFL night match kicks off in Melbourne at $7\text{:30 pm}$ (`1930`). Find the local kick-off time in Perth and in Adelaide: (a) in July, when Melbourne is on AEST ($\text{UTC}+10$), Adelaide is on ACST ($\text{UTC}+9.5$), and Perth is on AWST ($\text{UTC}+8$); (b) in October during Daylight Saving, when Melbourne is on AEDT ($\text{UTC}+11$), Adelaide is on ACDT ($\text{UTC}+10.5$), and Perth remains on AWST ($\text{UTC}+8$).

steps.thinking: In July (Standard Time), Perth ($\text{UTC}+8$) is $10 - 8 = 2\text{ hours}$ behind Melbourne ($\text{UTC}+10$), and Adelaide ($\text{UTC}+9.5$) is $10 - 9.5 = 0.5\text{ hours}$ ($30\text{ minutes}$) behind Melbourne.
steps.working: $$\text{(a) July: Perth} = 7\text{:30 pm} - 2\text{ h} = 5\text{:30 pm (1730)}; \quad \text{Adelaide} = 7\text{:30 pm} - 30\text{ min} = 7\text{:00 pm (1900)}$$

steps.thinking: In October (Daylight Saving), Melbourne is at $\text{UTC}+11$, so Perth ($\text{UTC}+8$) is now $11 - 8 = 3\text{ hours}$ behind Melbourne, while Adelaide ($\text{UTC}+10.5$) is still $11 - 10.5 = 30\text{ minutes}$ behind Melbourne.
steps.working: $$\text{(b) October: Perth} = 7\text{:30 pm} - 3\text{ h} = 4\text{:30 pm (1630)}; \quad \text{Adelaide} = 7\text{:30 pm} - 30\text{ min} = 7\text{:00 pm (1900)}$$

worked_examples.final_answer: (a) July: Perth $5\text{:30 pm}$ (`1730`), Adelaide $7\text{:00 pm}$ (`1900`); (b) October: Perth $4\text{:30 pm}$ (`1630`), Adelaide $7\text{:00 pm}$ (`1900`)

now_you_try.problem: During summer (January), Sydney is on AEDT ($\text{UTC}+11$), Brisbane is on AEST ($\text{UTC}+10$), and Darwin is on ACST ($\text{UTC}+9.5$). When it is $2\text{:15 pm}$ (`1415`) in Sydney, what is the local time in Brisbane and in Darwin?
now_you_try.hint: Brisbane is $1\text{ hour}$ behind AEDT, and Darwin is $1.5\text{ hours}$ ($1\text{ h } 30\text{ min}$) behind AEDT.
now_you_try.working_summary: Brisbane: $2\text{:15 pm} - 1\text{ h} = 1\text{:15 pm}$ (`1315`). Darwin: $2\text{:15 pm} - 1\text{ h } 30\text{ min} = 12\text{:45 pm}$ (`1245`).

worked_examples.title: Calculating International Flight Arrival Time and Duration
worked_examples.problem: A Qantas flight departs Melbourne (AEST, $\text{UTC}+10$) at $11\text{:20 am}$ on Tuesday and flies to Singapore ($\text{UTC}+8$). The flight duration is $7\text{ hours } 50\text{ minutes}$. What is the local time in Singapore when the aircraft lands?

steps.thinking: Convert the departure time into Singapore local time first. Since Singapore ($\text{UTC}+8$) is $10 - 8 = 2\text{ hours}$ behind Melbourne ($\text{UTC}+10$), subtract $2\text{ hours}$ from $11\text{:20 am}$.
steps.working: $$\text{Departure in Singapore time} = 11\text{:20 am} - 2\text{ hours} = 9\text{:20 am (0920) on Tuesday}$$

steps.thinking: Add the flight duration of $7\text{ hours } 50\text{ minutes}$ to the Singapore departure time `09:20`.
steps.working: $$09\text{:20} + 7\text{ h } 50\text{ min} = 16\text{ h } 70\text{ min} = 17\text{:10 (5:10 pm on Tuesday)}$$

now_you_try.problem: A flight departs Perth (AWST, $\text{UTC}+8$) at $1\text{:40 pm}$ (`1340`) and lands in Auckland ($\text{UTC}+12$) after a flight of $6\text{ hours } 30\text{ minutes}$. Find the local arrival time in Auckland.
now_you_try.hint: Auckland ($\text{UTC}+12$) is $12 - 8 = 4\text{ hours}$ ahead of Perth. Convert departure to Auckland time first, then add $6\text{ h } 30\text{ min}$.
now_you_try.working_summary: Departure in Auckland time $= 13\text{:40} + 4\text{ h} = 17\text{:40}$ ($5\text{:40 pm}$). Add $6\text{ h } 30\text{ min}$: $17\text{:40} + 6\text{:30} = 24\text{:10} = 00\text{:10}$ ($12\text{:10 am}$ the next day).

common_misconceptions.title: Subtracting Times as Base-10 Decimals Instead of Base-60 Hours and Minutes
common_misconceptions.misconception: Treating `15:20 - 12:45` as ordinary decimal subtraction $15.20 - 12.45 = 2.75$ and claiming the duration is $2\text{ hours } 75\text{ minutes}$ (or $2\text{ hours } 45\text{ minutes}$).
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: There are $60\text{ minutes}$ in $1\text{ hour}$, not $100$. When borrowing $1\text{ hour}$ from the hours column, add $60\text{ minutes}$ to the minutes column ($20 + 60 = 80\text{ minutes}$).
common_misconceptions.correct_working: $$15\text{ h } 20\text{ min} = 14\text{ h } 80\text{ min}; \quad (14 - 12)\text{ h } (80 - 45)\text{ min} = 2\text{ h } 35\text{ min}$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: From $12\text{:45 pm}$ to $1\text{:00 pm}$ is $15\text{ min}$, and from $1\text{:00 pm}$ to $3\text{:20 pm}$ is $2\text{ h } 20\text{ min}$, giving $2\text{ h } 35\text{ min}$.

common_misconceptions.title: Confusing 12:00 am (Midnight) and 12:00 pm (Noon) in 24-Hour Time
common_misconceptions.misconception: Writing $12\text{:15 am}$ as `1215` or adding $12$ to $12\text{:15 pm}$ to get `2415`.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: The new day begins at $12\text{:00 am}$ (midnight), which has $00$ hours (`0000`), so $12\text{:15 am}$ is `0015`. Midday ($12\text{:00 pm}$) is already $12$ hours into the day, so $12\text{:15 pm}$ is `1215`.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: One minute after $11\text{:59 am}$ (`1159`) is $12\text{:00 pm}$ (`1200`), and one minute after $11\text{:59 pm}$ (`2359`) is $12\text{:00 am}$ (`0000`).

fluency_and_understanding.question: Convert the following 12-hour times into four-digit 24-hour time: (a) $7\text{:08 am}$, (b) $3\text{:45 pm}$, (c) $12\text{:25 am}$, (d) $12\text{:50 pm}$.
step_by_step_solution: For $7\text{:08 am}$, place a leading zero: `0708`. For $3\text{:45 pm}$, add $12$ to the hour ($3 + 12 = 15$): `1545`.
For $12\text{:25 am}$ (after midnight), the hour is $00$: `0025`. For $12\text{:50 pm}$ (after noon), the hour stays $12$: `1250`.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Calculate the elapsed time (in hours and minutes) from $8\text{:38 am}$ to $4\text{:15 pm}$ on the same day.
step_by_step_solution: Convert $4\text{:15 pm}$ to 24-hour time: `16:15`. Rewrite `16:15` by borrowing $1\text{ hour} = 60\text{ minutes}$: $15\text{ h } 75\text{ min}$.
Subtract `08:38`: $(15 - 8)\text{ h } (75 - 38)\text{ min} = 7\text{ hours } 37\text{ minutes}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: A documentary starts at `19:45` ($7\text{:45 pm}$) and runs for $2\text{ hours } 35\text{ minutes}$. At what time does it finish (give your answer in both 24-hour and 12-hour time)?
step_by_step_solution: Add hours and minutes: $19\text{ h } 45\text{ min} + 2\text{ h } 35\text{ min} = 21\text{ h } 80\text{ min}$.
Since $80\text{ min} = 1\text{ h } 20\text{ min}$, the finish time is $22\text{:20}$ (`2220`), which is $10\text{:20 pm}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: During winter (Standard Time), Hobart is on AEST ($\text{UTC}+10$), Darwin is on ACST ($\text{UTC}+9.5$), and Broome is on AWST ($\text{UTC}+8$). If a live webinar starts in Broome at $10\text{:45 am}$ (`1045`), what is the local start time in (a) Darwin and (b) Hobart?
step_by_step_solution: Darwin ($\text{UTC}+9.5$) is $9.5 - 8 = 1.5\text{ hours}$ ($1\text{ h } 30\text{ min}$) ahead of Broome ($\text{UTC}+8$): $10\text{:45 am} + 1\text{ h } 30\text{ min} = 12\text{:15 pm}$ (`1215`).
Hobart ($\text{UTC}+10$) is $10 - 8 = 2\text{ hours}$ ahead of Broome: $10\text{:45 am} + 2\text{ h} = 12\text{:45 pm}$ (`1245`).

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: In January (summer), a business executive in Melbourne (AEDT, $\text{UTC}+11$) wants to schedule a $45$-minute video call with a colleague in Perth (AWST, $\text{UTC}+8$) and a colleague in Brisbane (AEST, $\text{UTC}+10$). If the call begins at $9\text{:00 am}$ Perth time, at what local time does the call **end** in Melbourne and in Brisbane?
problem_solving_and_modelling.final_answer: Melbourne: ends at $12\text{:45 pm}$ (`1245`); Brisbane: ends at $11\text{:45 am}$ (`1145`)
step_by_step_solution: At $9\text{:00 am}$ in Perth ($\text{UTC}+8$), the call starts at $9\text{:00 am} + 3\text{ h} = 12\text{:00 pm}$ (noon) in Melbourne ($\text{UTC}+11$) and $9\text{:00 am} + 2\text{ h} = 11\text{:00 am}$ in Brisbane ($\text{UTC}+10$).
Adding the $45$-minute duration gives an end time of $12\text{:45 pm}$ (`1245`) in Melbourne and $11\text{:45 am}$ (`1145`) in Brisbane.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A non-stop flight from Perth (AWST, $\text{UTC}+8$) to London ($	ext{UTC}+0$) departs Perth at $6\text{:50 pm}$ (`1850`) on Wednesday and takes $17\text{ hours } 20\text{ minutes}$. Find the local time and day in London when the flight lands.
step_by_step_solution: Convert the departure time to London time ($\text{UTC}+0$, which is $8\text{ hours}$ behind Perth): $18\text{:50} - 8\text{ h} = 10\text{:50 am}$ (`1050`) on Wednesday.

Add the $17\text{ h } 20\text{ min}$ flight time: $10\text{:50} + 17\text{:20} = 27\text{ h } 70\text{ min} = 28\text{:10}$. Subtracting $24\text{ hours}$ gives $04\text{:10}$ ($4\text{:10 am}$) on Thursday.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A flight departs Sydney (AEST, $\text{UTC}+10$) at $9\text{:30 am}$ on Monday and lands in Tokyo ($\text{UTC}+9$) at $6\text{:15 pm}$ (`1815`) on Monday (Tokyo local time). How long was the flight in hours and minutes?
problem_solving_and_modelling.context: Finding Flight Duration Across Time Zones
step_by_step_solution: Convert the Sydney departure time into Tokyo local time ($\text{UTC}+9$ is $1\text{ hour}$ behind $\text{UTC}+10$): $9\text{:30 am} - 1\text{ h} = 8\text{:30 am}$ (`08:30`) Tokyo time.

Find the duration from `08:30` to `18:15` in Tokyo time: $18\text{ h } 15\text{ min} - 8\text{ h } 30\text{ min} = 17\text{ h } 75\text{ min} - 8\text{ h } 30\text{ min} = 9\text{ hours } 45\text{ minutes}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: An Adelaide hospital nurse works a night shift starting at $10\text{:45 pm}$ (`2245`) on Tuesday and finishing at $7\text{:15 am}$ (`0715`) on Wednesday, with an unpaid $30$-minute meal break during the shift. If she is paid $\$44$ per hour for her paid working time, calculate (a) her paid working duration in hours and (b) her total pay for the shift.
step_by_step_solution: From $10\text{:45 pm}$ to midnight is $1\text{ h } 15\text{ min}$, plus $7\text{ h } 15\text{ min}$ after midnight gives $8\text{ h } 30\text{ min}$ total time on site.
Subtract the $30$-minute unpaid break to get $8\text{ hours}$ of paid work. Total pay $= 8 \times \$44 = \$352$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: A flight leaves Auckland ($\text{UTC}+12$) at $7\text{:00 am}$ on Friday and flies east across the International Date Line to Honolulu ($\text{UTC}-10$). The flight takes $8\text{ hours } 30\text{ minutes}$. Show that the plane lands in Honolulu on **Thursday** (the day before it took off!), and find its exact local arrival time.
step_by_step_solution: Find the time offset from Auckland ($\text{UTC}+12$) to Honolulu ($\text{UTC}-10$): $-10 - 12 = -22\text{ hours}$ (Honolulu is $22\text{ hours}$ behind Auckland).

At departure ($7\text{:00 am}$ Friday in Auckland), add the $8\text{ h } 30\text{ min}$ flight in Auckland time to get $3\text{:30 pm}$ (`15:30`) Friday, then subtract $22\text{ hours}$ (which is equivalent to adding $2\text{ hours}$ and going back $1$ full day): $15\text{:30} + 2\text{ h} = 17\text{:30}$ ($5\text{:30 pm}$) on Thursday.

reasoning_and_communication.question: In summer, Broken Hill (NSW) uses Central Daylight Time (ACDT, $\text{UTC}+10.5$), whereas Coolangatta (QLD) uses Eastern Standard Time (AEST, $\text{UTC}+10$), even though Coolangatta lies further east geographically than Broken Hill. Explain which town has a later clock time in January and by how many minutes.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Broken Hill (ACDT, $\text{UTC}+10.5$) is $30\text{ minutes}$ ahead of Coolangatta (AEST, $\text{UTC}+10$) in January
step_by_step_solution: Compare the UTC offsets in January: Broken Hill is at $\text{UTC}+10.5$ because it observes daylight saving, while Queensland stays on standard time at $\text{UTC}+10$.
Since $10.5 - 10 = +0.5\text{ hours} = 30\text{ minutes}$, Broken Hill's clocks are $30\text{ minutes}$ ahead of Coolangatta's in summer.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Liam calculates the number of minutes between `09:50` and `12:10` by computing $1210 - 950 = 260\text{ minutes}$. Explain mathematically why subtracting four-digit 24-hour integers always overestimates the duration by $40\text{ minutes}$ for every hour boundary crossed, and use this rule to correct Liam's answer.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Each hour boundary jumps by $100 - 60 = 40$ in four-digit notation (e.g. `0959` to `1000` jumps by $41$ instead of $1$). Since `09:50` to `12:10` crosses $3$ hour boundaries ($10\text{:00}, 11\text{:00}, 12\text{:00}$), the true duration is $260 - 3 \times 40 = 140\text{ minutes}$ ($2\text{ h } 20\text{ min}$).
step_by_step_solution: In four-digit 24-hour notation, $1\text{ hour}$ increases the number by $100$, whereas $1\text{ hour}$ is actually $60\text{ minutes}$ — an excess of $100 - 60 = 40$ per hour boundary.

From `09:50` to `12:10` crosses $12 - 9 = 3$ hour boundaries, so subtracting $3 \times 40 = 120$ from $260$ gives the true duration: $260 - 120 = 140\text{ minutes}$ ($2\text{ hours } 20\text{ minutes}$).

reasoning_and_communication.question: Earth rotates through $360^\circ$ of longitude every $24\text{ hours}$. (a) Through how many degrees of longitude does Earth rotate in $1\text{ hour}$, and how many minutes of time correspond to $1^\circ$ of longitude? (b) Melbourne lies near longitude $145^\circ\text{ E}$ and Perth lies near $116^\circ\text{ E}$. Based purely on solar longitude, what is the true solar time difference (in hours and minutes) between Melbourne and Perth?
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: (a) $15^\circ$ per hour ($4\text{ minutes}$ per degree of longitude); (b) $1\text{ hour } 56\text{ minutes}$ ($116\text{ minutes}$)
step_by_step_solution: In $1\text{ hour}$, Earth rotates $\frac{360^\circ}{24} = 15^\circ$. Each $1^\circ$ of longitude corresponds to $\frac{60\text{ min}}{15} = 4\text{ minutes}$ of solar time.

The longitude difference is $145^\circ - 116^\circ = 29^\circ$. Multiplying by $4\text{ minutes/degree}$ gives $29 \times 4 = 116\text{ minutes} = 1\text{ hour } 56\text{ minutes}$ (which is why WA and the eastern states have a $2$-hour standard time difference).
